topic: software supply-chain security; CI/CD; SBOMs; intrusion detection
status: bounded candidate research opportunity from six fixed-frame audits, with targeted support and counterevidence; not evidence controls are ineffective
claim: In this audited slice, multiple studies measure an intermediate artifact or benchmark signal rather than downstream harm: GitHub workflow edits (including pinning/permissions), practitioner reports about SBOM/provenance processes, and anomaly-detector scores on public IDS datasets. Those are useful outcomes for their stated questions, but they do not establish that a control reduced real compromises, shortened remediation, or improved operator decisions. This creates a testable opportunity to link deployment of security controls to independently adjudicated operational outcomes instead of treating configuration compliance or benchmark recall as a substitute endpoint.
positive_evidence: The 49,258-repository GitHub Actions study measures workflow histories and reports pinning/permission changes, but its outcomes are file-change patterns; it does not link them to incidents or exploits.

The 17-practitioner/13-agency summit summary reports that SBOM production is ahead of actionable consumption and leaves SBOM benefit/use cases as open questions; it is qualitative panel evidence, not a measured effect.

XION reports detection and runtime comparisons on two pre-collected CIC datasets, but its authors identify dataset/label/flow-construction limits and call for controlled known-cause testbeds, drift work, and operational validation.

The MESO camouflaging paper estimates a substantial delay penalty alongside area/power savings and leaves control circuitry/fabricated system validation for future work, illustrating that component-level security claims can leave integration costs unresolved.
counterevidence: The GitHub Actions paper is a large and carefully described longitudinal dataset, and directly establishes how workflow configurations evolve even though it does not estimate incident prevention.

XION evaluates two separate benchmark datasets, performs sensitivity analysis, reports attack-specific strengths and a weaker SSH brute-force case, and is meaningful empirical evidence within that benchmark scope.
The component papers were designed for narrower questions; absence of downstream outcomes in these papers is not proof that no other literature has studied them or that controls do not work.

sources.sections: dataset, security-related workflow edits, threats to validity
summit method, SBOM/provenance discussion, open questions
two-dataset results and threats to validity
PPA estimates, security threat model, future work

falsifiable_test: Run a preregistered stepped-wedge or matched rollout of a defined CI hardening bundle (pinned actions, least-privilege permissions, SBOM generation plus consumption workflow, and provenance verification) across multiple organizations. Link adoption and compliance to independently verified vulnerable-dependency exposure, incident/exploit occurrence, time-to-detection/remediation, false-positive burden, and developer effort. Treat SBOM coverage and workflow edits as mediators, not final outcomes; predeclare incident adjudication and confounder controls. The opportunity weakens if existing multi-organization evaluations already establish comparable downstream causal effects or if the intervention produces no risk/response improvement at realistic adoption levels.
limitations: This is a purposive synthesis across six heterogeneous full texts, not a systematic review of all supply-chain security literature. No pooled effect is calculated; no incident database has yet been linked to these studies. The objective relies on one potentially small number of adjudicable incidents, so time-to-remediation and exposure windows may be more statistically tractable outcomes than breach counts.
